Furthermore, if the form of the Lord’s Supper is the entire action, including the things being received—both earthly and heavenly—as Valentinus himself confesses, it follows necessarily that the impious do not have the sacrament itself, because they have neither faith, the primary part of the Supper's action, nor the body and blood of Christ, the primary matter of the Supper. Eunomius, Apollinarius, Bonosus, and in older times Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, and Cerinthus, and many others who were not anathematized during their lives, were condemned after death. They are anathematized by the Catholic Church because they died in their own error. translation: standing near the man of fire, and he himself sought refuge in Lawrence. And Lawrence pleaded with the man of fire to spare him. And he said: "Let me kill this one, as his companions, for he is an enemy of Christ and a persecutor of His servants. Do you vouch for him, that he shall turn from his evils and seek refuge in the power of the cross of Christ?" And Lawrence said: "If he comes to me and seeks refuge in Christ, I will vouch for him." And Agrippas shouted: "Yes, my lord, I renounce the idols and I confess Christ; have mercy on me, my lord, I beseech you." And at that moment, he removed the spear from him, and putting a yoke around his neck, dragged him and took him into a chasm full of unquenchable fire and darkness and stench, in which Agrippas saw all the heads of the idols whom he knew and recognized before. And the angel said to him: "It is necessary for you to be cast in because of your lawlessness." And Agrippas, looking, saw Lawrence from afar, and shouting, he said: "O merciful father, have mercy on me and save me." And he came and stood between him and the cherub, and with supplications, he took him from him. And the cherub said: "Behold, I give him to you until I see what he shall do." And stretching out his hands, he said: "See the martyrs of Christ whom you killed for the sake of Christ, for behold, they are brightened with fiery crowns." And Agrippas, looking at the holy martyrs who had been killed first, saw that they were reigning with unspeakable glory and were resting in the garden of light and the kingdom of heaven. <summary>Agrippas experiences a terrifying prophetic dream of his own judgment, where Lawrence intercedes for his soul, offering a glimpse of the glory of the martyrs.</summary> <keywords>Agrippas, Lawrence, dream, martyrdom, Christ, cross, heaven, mercy</keywords>

translation: In general; then, to investigate their origin. Leaving aside the hidden qualities of the ancients, I proceed to the opinions of our own times, which are enlightened by the clearest physical knowledge. Of these, there are two primary ones: the first is Cartesian, confirmed and explained by Huygens; the second originated with Gassendi and gained importance through the agreement and interpretation of Newton. The difference between both opinions lies in their views on movement. In both, a thinnest, fluid, and altogether intangible matter is posited. However, the movement according to Newton is considered to be a flow, pouring out from luminous bodies in all directions like a river; according to Descartes, it is posited as being consta

it, which may or may not actually exist; this will be revealed later. The first movement may be a flow or passage, as Gassendi and Newton believe, by which the Aether (I call the matter of Light this, along with the ancients and many moderns) moves from the sun and from other great and small luminous bodies in all directions, like a river, constantly. The second movement in the Aether may be a vibration, according to the opinion of Descartes and Huygens, by which it acts in all directions from the sun like very small and frequent waves, extending them through the Ocean of universal space filled with matter. translation: ### Chapter XIX came out under Augustine's name. Whoever, therefore, recognizes how far Augustine's presentation of the doctrines of Christianity reaches, will also be able to test Anselm's works well. ### XXXIX. BRUNO. 1. His history, and 2. writings. 1. Bruno, called Astensis to distinguish him from the founder of the Carthusian Order, after his noble family, was a bishop in France. He later resigned, yet was forced to take up his office again. He later resigned a second time and became abbot in the Cassinese monastery <note>Monte Cassino</note> in the year 1107. After this, he nonetheless had to take up his bishopric again in the year 1111 and finally died in the year 1125. See Peter the Deacon in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* <note>original: "Chron. Cassinensi"</note>. 2. From him we have many interpretations of the Bible, which are not to be rejected, such as: On the five books of Moses, On Job, The Psalter, The Song of Solomon, The Revelation of John. Likewise, 145 sermons. A book on the Song of Zacharias, and several other small works, which are also found among those of Bruno the Carthusian. The sermons are particularly noteworthy because they were very often published and cited under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, until Mauro Marchesi vindicated <gloss>identified and claimed</gloss> them in Venice, 1651, in two volumes. <summary>This page concludes the discussion of Anselm's connection to Augustine and introduces Bruno of Asti, a bishop and abbot known for his biblical commentaries and sermons that were long misattributed.</summary> <keywords>Anselm of Canterbury, Saint Augustine, Bruno of Asti, Monte Cassino, biblical commentary, Eusebius of Emesa</keywords>

Bruno, however, did not endure long in the clamor of this court and turned to Calabria, where he established the second monastery of his Order at Torre in the year 1094. He lived there until his day of death, which was October 6, 1101. Leo X placed him among the saints of the Roman Church in the year 1514. ### Writings. The similarity of the name has caused many to attribute to our Bruno a considerable number of writings that did not come from his pen. Of this kind are the small treatises and the homilies that one finds printed in the editions of the works of the Carthusian. They belong properly to Bishop Bruno of Segni. The books that the critics attribute to our writer are: 1. *Commentarius in Psalmos* <note>Commentary on the Psalms</note>. The authors of the *Literary History of France* give him great praise. One must distinguish it well from similar works by Bishop Bruno of Würzburg and Bishop Bruno of Segni. 2. *Expositio in omnes epistolas D. Pauli* <note>Exposition on all the epistles of St. Paul</note>. 3. *Epistolae duae ad Radulphum Viridem*, <note>Two letters to Radulphus Viridis</note> provost of the church of Reims, and to his brothers inhabiting the hermitage of the Great Chartreuse. 4. *Elegia de contemtu mundi* <note>Elegy on the contempt of the world</note>. 5. *Confessio fidei* <note>Confession of faith</note>, which he laid down shortly before his death. <summary>This page recounts Bruno's later life in Rome and Calabria, his canonization, and clarifies the attribution of his authentic writings against those erroneously attributed to him.</summary> <keywords>Bruno, Urban II, Calabria, canonization, bibliography, authentic vs. spurious works</keywords>

Let us come to the Carthusians, whose beginning falls in the year of salvation 1080. For a certain man of singular learning, named Bruno, a man of Cologne, while he was teaching philosophy at Paris, it happened that he seemed to hear a certain friend, endowed with good morals and now deceased, crying out before he was given to burial: "By the just judgment of God, I am damned." Moved by that thing, he immediately, with six companions terrified by the same miraculous event, seeking the deserts of the wilderness, arrived in the diocese of Grenoble (it is a city of the Celts), and there chose a place which today has the name of the Chartreuse <note>original: "Carthusia"</note>, which Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, took care to assign to him, who immediately joined himself to that family. translation: <header>Book II Prose VIII</header> <margin></margin> Note that Fabricius was a Roman consul who, when he was sent to fight against Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes, the king promised him a part of his kingdom if he would come over to him. Fabricius scorned this. The following year, Pyrrhus offered him a great sum of gold to betray Rome to him. To whom Fabricius said: "Rome does not want gold, but wants to overcome its enemies or men." For this reason he was called the faithful Fabricius. When a physician had come, promising to kill King Pyrrhus if Fabricius would give him some money, Fabricius himself sent this traitor of the king bound to Pyrrhus to be punished for such a crime. To whom Pyrrhus then prayed: "It is more possible for the sun to deviate from its path than for Fabricius to depart from the paths of right reason." translation: his word "renounce" can in no way carry the meaning that they intend. Rather, the Pope intends nothing other than this: namely, that his works are not accepted as authentic in the Church, nor is he himself received as an approved teacher whose sayings are to be believed in the Church. Even if the Pope had not only said "we hold back" but "we damn," it would be of no use to them, because we are also accustomed to speak this way: "In this matter **Scotus** damns **Thomas**," or "**Hervaeus** damns Scotus," <note>Pico refers to the famous intellectual battles between scholastic theologians Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, and Hervaeus Natalis. To "damn" a person in an academic context meant to reject their arguments or doctrines, not to judge their eternal soul.</note> and so on for the rest. In these phrases, we must always understand the "damnation" of the doctrine and not the soul, according to the common and proper way of speaking. <summary>Pico argues that the Church's historical condemnation of Origen refers to his heretical writings and status as an unapproved teacher, not a final judgment on his soul's salvation, which only God can determine. He explains that medieval academic language often used "damn" to mean the refutation of ideas rather than eternal punishment.</summary> <keywords>Origen, Pope Gelasius, salvation, damnation, Church authority, heresy, scholasticism, Duns Scotus, Thomas Aquinas, canon law</keywords>
